source.title: The Virtue of Complexity in Return Prediction
source.authors: Bryan Kelly; S. Malamud; Kangying Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The study tests model-complexity effects on out-of-sample risk using random Fourier feature ridge regressions and theoretical high-dimensional regressions, rather than reproducing the original deep-network training method.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own out-of-sample R2 sweeps over model complexity and discusses recovery past the interpolation boundary. It also reports complexity effects on market-timing returns and Sharpe ratios, which are not test-error measures; the Sharpe-ratio result is recorded under fits_no_version. Double-descent results cited from other work are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own out-of-sample R2 curves against model complexity for random Fourier feature (RFF) ridge regressions on US market-return data. It also derives random-matrix limits for ridge(less) regression. These results show the error peak at P=T, recovery beyond it, and removal of the peak under optimal shrinkage, all in a new finance setting. It trains no deep networks, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors prove and document that, for misspecified models, out-of-sample R2 and Sharpe ratio rise with complexity beyond P=T, and that optimal shrinkage adds further gains. They argue that R2 understates economic value. They frame the double-descent-like Sharpe hump as an artifact of insufficient shrinkage.
record.recipe_differences: The empirical models are random Fourier feature regressions with fixed random first-layer weights and ridge regression; the paper also develops random-matrix-theory results for linear ridge regression. It does not train deep networks across sizes using the original deep-network recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies training-window length, ridge shrinkage, feature count, and RFF bandwidth. It reports that the broad patterns persist for training windows of 12, 60, and 120 months and for alternative bandwidths.

fits_no_version.finding: Market-timing Sharpe ratio generally rises with complexity, dipping briefly near c=1 at low shrinkage. Theory calls Sharpe 'double ascent' an artifact of insufficient shrinkage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Portfolio Sharpe ratio mirrors double descent as 'double ascent', which optimal ridge shrinkage turns into monotone ascent.

record.problems: The empirical risk curves are presented primarily in figures, without stated numeric values or uncertainty estimates for those curves. The empirical neural-network-like architecture uses fixed random first-layer weights rather than a fully trained deep network. Some theoretical comparisons vary the complexity of the true DGP along with model complexity.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant risk-sweep outcomes were left out. The paper's many reported return, volatility, recession-timing, and Sharpe results are outside the tested error/risk versions, except for the Sharpe-ratio trend recorded as R6.

untested.parts: Not tested: no trained deep networks. The RFF model is random features with a fixed first layer.
Not tested: training epochs are not varied.
Not tested: sample size near the threshold is not varied as a test. Longer windows in Table 1 lower the complexity ratio rather than test whether more data hurts.
Only ridge and random-feature regressions are tested; no other model classes.
Not tested: no single effective-complexity measure across axes.
Label-noise dependence and triple or multiple descent are untested. Only the variance role and removal of the peak by shrinkage are tested.
Not tested: complexity is not re-expressed as an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Misspecified-model ridgeless theory (true complexity c=10): R2 dives near cq=1 and recovers for cq>1, similar to Fig. 1.
Correctly specified theory: optimal shrinkage z*=c/b* gives positive R2 at every complexity, removing the c=1 collapse; z>0 curves improve R2 except at very low complexity.
Empirical R2 zoom: with high z, R2 is almost everywhere positive across all training windows, so the boundary dip is dampened by regularization.
Linear kitchen-sink regression near the boundary (P=15, T=12): ridgeless R2 below −100% versus −3.8% with z=10^3.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3: a new finance setting using a standard random-features method. V1 links were removed because RFF is not a trained deep network. The V4 limits_scope label from R5 was dropped; R5 bears on V6 instead. Empirical curves are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fully trained deep networks; its empirical neural-network-like model uses random Fourier features with fixed first-layer weights.
Does not vary training epochs or measure test error over training time.
Does not test whether increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold raises test error.
Tests ridge-regression and random-feature settings, not a broad set of model classes.
Does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Tests regularization effects on risk curves, but not label-noise dependence or triple/multiple descent.
Does not re-express complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether doing so converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random Fourier feature (RFF) model
rows.operation_detail: Sweep the number of random Fourier features and measure recursive out-of-sample prediction performance.
rows.locator: Section 6.3, Figure 7 Panel A; Section 6.3 text
rows.note: The text describes explosive behavior at the interpolation boundary and recovery in the high-complexity regime. It does not give numeric values for the curve or explicitly describe the entire low-to-high-complexity shape.
rows.check: RFF ridge regression is a two-layer random-features model with a fixed first layer, not a deep network, so V1 does not apply. For low shrinkage (z≈10^-3) the text reports explosive R2 at the interpolation boundary and recovery at high complexity, and says this closely matches theory. That is the full V4 shape, so 'partial' understates it. The row merges ridge penalties from 10^-3 to 10^3; the higher-z curves (Fig. 14) bear on V6.

rows.subject: correctly specified ridge regression model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze limiting out-of-sample R2 as model complexity c varies.
rows.value: R2(0;c) deteriorates as c approaches 1 from below, tends to −∞ as c→1, rises for c>1, and tends to 0 as c→∞.
rows.locator: Proposition 3, equation (14) and equation (15); Section 4.1 and Figure 1 discussion
rows.note: The authors describe deterioration below the interpolation boundary and recovery beyond it. In this comparative static, complexity of the correctly specified model also changes the true DGP.
rows.check: Correct as recorded. Caveat: in this comparative static the true DGP's complexity changes along with the model's, and the result assumes H(0+)=0. The same proposition's optimal-shrinkage result (z*=c/b*, positive R2 everywhere) is not recorded.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Proposition 3, equations (14)–(15), pp. 20–23; Section 5, p. 29.

rows.subject: misspecified ridge regression model
rows.size_stated: Observed-signal count P1 with P1/P = q
rows.operation_detail: Expand the empirical model's observed-signal subset and use the study's optimal ridge shrinkage.
rows.value: Strictly monotone increasing and concave in q ∈ [0,1].
rows.note: This result is for a fixed true DGP approximated by expanding, misspecified empirical models. Under the stated optimal shrinkage, the risk curve increases with q rather than exhibiting a peak.
rows.check: Under optimal shrinkage, R2 rises monotonically with no peak, which is what V6's regularization clause predicts. It does not qualify V4, which concerns the interpolating regime, so the V4 link is removed.
